description: Real GDP growth: how much more the economy produced than the year before, with inflation taken out.
The size of the economy: everything it produced in the year, converted to US dollars at the year's average exchange rate.
The size of the economy at purchasing power parity, which adjusts for prices differing between countries.
The country's share of the world economy, at purchasing power parity.
Everything the economy produced in the year, at that year's prices, in the country's own currency.
GDP with inflation taken out, in the country's own currency. Real growth is its percent change.
GDP at current prices over the government's fiscal year, the base for fiscal ratios where that year is not the calendar year.
The output gap: how far the economy runs above (positive) or below (negative) what it could produce. Reported for some advanced economies.
GDP in US dollars divided by population: a rough measure of average income.
GDP per person at purchasing power parity, which adjusts for prices differing between countries: the usual measure for comparing living standards.
GDP per person at purchasing power parity with inflation taken out, for comparing living standards over time.
GDP per person at current prices, in the country's own currency.
GDP per person with inflation taken out, in the country's own currency.
The purchasing power parity rate: how many units of the country's currency buy what one US dollar buys in the United States.
Inflation: how much consumer prices rose on average over the year. The headline measure.
Inflation measured from the end of one year to the end of the next.
The level of consumer prices, averaged over the year.
The level of consumer prices at the end of the year.
The price level of everything in GDP. Its change is a broad measure of inflation.
The number of people living in the country.
The unemployment rate: the share of people who want a job and do not have one. Many lower-income countries do not report it.
The number of people with a job. Reported mostly for advanced economies.
The current account balance as a share of the economy: what the country earns from the rest of the world minus what it pays. Negative means a deficit.
The current account balance in dollars: trade in goods and services, income and transfers with the rest of the world.
Growth in the volume of goods and services the country exports.
Growth in the volume of goods the country exports.
Growth in the volume of goods and services the country imports.
Growth in the volume of goods the country imports.
National savings: what households, firms and the government save together, as a share of the economy.
Investment: spending on buildings, machines, infrastructure and inventories, as a share of the economy.
Government revenue as a share of the economy: taxes, social contributions, grants and other income.
Government spending as a share of the economy, interest included.
The overall balance: government revenue minus all spending, as a share of the economy. Negative means a deficit.
The primary balance: the overall balance with interest left out, both the interest the government pays and the interest it earns. Primary minus overall is net interest.
The structural balance: the government's balance adjusted for the ups and downs of the business cycle. Reported for fewer than half of countries.
Gross government debt as a share of the economy: everything the government owes. The most quoted measure of public debt.
Net government debt as a share of the economy: gross debt minus the government's financial assets. Reported for fewer than half of countries.
Government revenue, in the country's own currency.
Government spending, interest included, in the country's own currency.
The overall balance, in the country's own currency. Negative means a deficit, which the government borrows to cover.
The primary balance, in the country's own currency.
The structural balance, in the country's own currency.
Gross government debt, in the country's own currency.
Net government debt, in the country's own currency.
